endorsements.quote: However, before broad clinical deployment, further validation of these algorithms is imperative to verify that the models perform well and as-expected when applied to real-life clinical data, especially in images that were acquired in other centers not contributing to the training sets, or in the same center but using different scanning protocols.

Differences in breast density distributions, imaging protocols, and population demographics may all influence algorithm performance, so broader evaluation across heterogeneous populations is essential before large-scale deployment.
Thus, algorithmic confidence should never substitute for clinical judgement.
Therefore, to trust AI interpretation of scans, continual revalidation of that AI system should occur.

unlisted_practices: Implement AI in care under explicit, auditable checkpoints, such as SPIRIT-AI for protocol reporting and DECIDE-AI for early clinical evaluation and human factors, with ongoing post-market monitoring and recalibration.

Use a confidence-based triage framework in which high-confidence AI outputs with supporting highlighted image features are flagged for second review, low-confidence outputs are not displayed, and intermediate-confidence outputs are shown without emphasis.
Validate AI imaging signatures against biological ground truth such as histopathology, molecular assays, or validated biomarkers rather than only against human perception.
Foster interdisciplinary collaboration among radiologists, AI developers, and biologists to build AI systems that link imaging signatures to validated disease markers and mechanisms.

screen.reason: This is a perspective article exploring differences in visual biases and perception between AI and radiologists in medical imaging.
